title: The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro Is One of My New Favorite Budget Vacuums
gist: Wired's review of Roborock's $800 Qrevo 2 Pro robot vacuum (on sale for $500) finds strong corner/edge cleaning and quiet operation but weak spot-detection of small objects and spills, positioning it as a budget runner-up to the reviewer's current pick, the Eufy Omni C28.

insights.claim: The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro launched at the end of August 2026 with a list price of $800 but had already been discounted to $500 within weeks of launch, indicating aggressive early promotional pricing in the budget robot vacuum segment.
insights.speaker: Nena Farrell
insights.so_what: Rapid discounting shortly after launch suggests thin realized price power in the sub-$1,000 robot vacuum category and heavy reliance on promotional pricing to drive volume.
insights.quote: This vacuum retails for $800, but it's already been spotted on sale for $500 since it launched a few weeks ago.

insights.claim: Roborock had left its affordable Qrevo line without updates for years while shifting R&D focus to novelty designs like the Saros Z70 (which has a robotic arm to grab socks), before returning to refresh the Qrevo line in 2026 with the Qrevo Curv and now the Qrevo 2 Pro.
insights.speaker: Nena Farrell
insights.so_what: Shows Roborock's product strategy oscillating between gimmick-driven flagship features and neglected core budget lines, a pattern investors in the crowded robot vacuum category should watch when assessing product-roadmap discipline.
insights.quote: The company has been more focused on more unique designs, such as the Saros Z70, which has an entire arm attached to it to grab your socks. These have a way to go before they're actually useful.

insights.claim: The Qrevo 2 Pro is positioned by the reviewer as a budget runner-up against the Eufy Omni C28, her current top affordable pick, indicating the sub-$1,000 robot vacuum market has at least two credible competing options from Roborock and Eufy (Anker-owned).
insights.speaker: Nena Farrell
insights.so_what: Signals a two-horse competitive dynamic at the budget price tier between Roborock and Anker's Eufy brand, relevant for tracking market share in the robot vacuum category.
insights.quote: It's headed to my guide to the best robot vacuums as a runner-up budget option against my current affordable pick, the Eufy C28 Omni.

themes.theme: AI features underdeliver relative to marketing

insights.claim: The Qrevo 2 Pro's AI-powered 'SmartPlan' feature, marketed to better clean the home, showed no noticeable difference from running a regular cleaning cycle during roughly two weeks of testing, and the device's AI does not detect spills or stains.
insights.speaker: Nena Farrell
insights.so_what: Illustrates a recurring gap between AI feature marketing and measurable consumer benefit in smart home hardware, a pattern relevant to evaluating AI-feature premiums across the category.
insights.quote: I haven't noticed a difference in using SmartPlan compared to just running a regular cycle... It's not the kind of AI that's going to spot spills and stains, though.

insights.claim: The Qrevo 2 Pro's FlexiArm mop and reversible side brush combination delivered strong edge and corner cleaning performance, successfully clearing a stashed Cheerio in a hard-to-reach corner in the reviewer's standard corner-cleaning test, though it still missed one of three test Cheerios overall.
insights.speaker: Nena Farrell
insights.so_what: Edge/corner cleaning remains a key differentiator consumers weigh when choosing among budget robot vacuums; Roborock's FlexiArm mechanism appears to be a competitive strength versus rivals.
insights.quote: I was impressed by the edge cleaning with the FlexiArm mop, and the reversible side brush... It didn't achieve a perfect corner score, missing one of the three Cheerios, but I've yet to meet a robot vacuum that can achieve all three.

insights.claim: The vacuum's obstacle-avoidance AI reliably detects large obstacles like furniture but fails to identify small items such as cords, cat toys, tissues, and flat table legs, in some cases dragging a cat toy across the room or shredding a tissue instead of vacuuming it.
insights.speaker: Nena Farrell
insights.so_what: Small-object detection remains an unsolved technical limitation even in newer robot vacuum generations, a durable weakness for buyers with pets or kids' toys to consider.
insights.quote: It did, however, take a cat toy for a ride around the room sitting in front of it, and shredded up a loose tissue all over my son's high-pile rug instead of vacuuming it up successfully.

insights.claim: The vacuum's sticky-spill cleaning was its weakest tested performance, requiring two passes to fully clean a spill, and an all-over clean covering a spill area sometimes left surrounding flooring feeling stickier than before.
insights.speaker: Nena Farrell
insights.so_what: Spill/stain handling is a common weak point at this price tier absent AI stain detection, useful benchmark when comparing budget vacuum mopping claims.
insights.quote: My sticky spill test was its weakest point, taking two tries to clean the spilled spots... doing an all-over clean that happened to include a big spill gave area around the spill a stickier feel than normal.

insights.claim: The Qrevo 2 Pro still struggles with flooring thresholds (e.g., hardwood-to-carpet transitions), leaving debris behind when crossing certain thresholds, an issue Wired has also observed on other Roborock models including the Qrevo Curv 2 and Saros 20.
insights.speaker: Nena Farrell
insights.so_what: A recurring, cross-model Roborock weakness at flooring thresholds suggests a persistent hardware/design limitation rather than a one-off unit issue, relevant to expectations for future Roborock releases.
insights.quote: It also still struggled with thresholds, which is an issue we've seen before on Roborock vacuums... My former colleague Adrienne So noted it when she tested both the Qrevo Curv 2 and the Saros 20 this year.
